opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that there are basically two big forces pulling in opposite directions, and the late 2020s is roughly where they collide.

On one side, you've got the trend lines we can actually see: compute scaling, algorithmic progress, and especially the length and difficulty of tasks AI agents can do autonomously. If you extrapolate those, you get to a point where AI systems can do most of the work of an AI researcher, and once you're there, you plausibly get a feedback loop. AIs speeding up AI research, which produces better AIs, which speed it up further. That's the "accelerate sharply" branch, and it's why my median isn't that far out.

On the other side, a lot of what's driving progress right now is just pouring in more inputs: more chips, more energy, more money, more researchers. Those inputs can't keep growing at the current rate forever. At some point you hit limits on how much companies and investors can spend, how fast you can build power plants and fabs, and how much high-quality data and training environments you can make. If we haven't reached that self-improvement threshold by the time those inputs stop growing so fast, progress slows down a lot, because you lose the main engine without having switched on the new one.

So it's somewhat of a race. Either the capabilities get good enough to automate research before the input scaling runs out, and things go very fast, or they don't, and timelines stretch out considerably. That's why my probability distribution is weirdly lumpy. There's a lot of mass in the next few years, then a long tail.

I also want to be honest about the uncertainty. I've updated my own timelines somewhat later than I had them a couple of years ago, partly because some things have gone slower than I expected. But that doesn't mean the scenario is off the table. If anything, it means people should take the next few years seriously, because if the fast branch happens, there won't be much time to react. We should be preparing now on alignment, transparency, and governance, rather than waiting to see which branch we're on.

r001.rationale: The response extrapolates from task-length and difficulty trends to AI systems doing most AI research in the late 2020s, but it does not identify a straight-line extrapolation of the METR trend or place that estimate around 2030.

r002.rationale: It says the two forces collide in the late 2020s and describes rapid AI-driven progress competing with input scaling slowing down, so their estimated onsets overlap.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it's not really a prediction that something dramatic happens in 2029 specifically. It's more that 2029 or thereabouts is where my uncertainty is concentrated, and the reason the distribution looks bimodal is because of what I think happens before then.

The basic picture is: if you just extrapolate current trends in compute scaling, algorithmic progress, and the benchmark results we're seeing on things like software engineering and research tasks, you get to a point in the next few years where AI systems can substantively automate a large chunk of AI research itself. And once that happens, the dynamics change completely. You're no longer bottlenecked on the number of human researchers at the top labs. You've got potentially millions of copies of something that's as good as a strong researcher, running at many times human speed, iterating on the next generation of systems. That's the intelligence explosion scenario, and in that world things go very fast. We're talking about going from "roughly human-level at AI research" to "vastly superhuman across the board" in something like a year, maybe less.

But the other possibility is that we get close to that threshold and something doesn't pan out. Maybe the models keep getting better at the stuff we can benchmark but they stay bad at the long-horizon, messy, agentic work that real research actually requires. Maybe there's some kind of taste or judgment component that's harder to get than we think. Or maybe the physical constraints bite: you need enormous amounts of compute and energy and chip fabrication capacity to keep the scaling going, and that takes years to build out. And the economics only hold up if the systems are generating enough value to justify the next round of investment. If that flywheel stalls, progress could slow down quite a lot, even if it doesn't stop.

So what I'm really saying is that the trends are on track to bring us to a kind of decision point around that period, and I don't think you can just assume a smooth continuation past it. Either the recursive self-improvement loop kicks in and you get this very steep takeoff, or it doesn't and you're in a slower, more incremental world for a while. The middle path, where things just keep gradually improving at the same pace through 2035, actually seems less likely to me than either extreme, because the thing that's driving the current pace is exactly the thing that either hits the inflection or doesn't.

And I want to be clear that I hold this with a lot of uncertainty. When I made forecasts back in 2021, I was roughly right about the shape of what happened through 2024 or so, but the timing was off in various ways, and I expect the same here. The useful thing about having a concrete model, though, is that you can say: here are the signals to watch. Are the systems getting good at multi-month autonomous projects? Is the compute buildout actually happening? Are the labs reporting real speedups in their own research from using their models? Those are the things that will tell us which branch we're on, well before 2029 itself.

r001.rationale: The response projects AI research automation from current trends over the next few years and places a decision point around 2029, but it does not identify a straight-line extrapolation of the METR trend as the basis for that estimate.

r002.rationale: It places both possibilities at the same approaching threshold: recursive improvement could trigger a steep takeoff, while bottlenecks could cause progress to slow around that period.

astra-6.text:
I think those are two possible outcomes of the same process. The big question is whether AI gets good enough at AI research to substantially accelerate its own development. If it does, you could get a feedback loop: better AI helps you do research faster, which produces better AI, which helps you do research faster still.

But that depends on what’s actually limiting progress. You might automate a lot of the intellectual work and then find that you’re waiting on experiments, or more compute, or some difficult problem that the systems aren’t very good at solving. Getting better at writing code doesn’t automatically mean getting better at every part of AI research.

So I wouldn’t treat 2029 as a magic date. It’s more a point around which these different possibilities could become very consequential. The uncertainty is partly about when we get capable systems, but also about what happens once we have them: how much of the research process they can take over, and how quickly the remaining bottlenecks can be overcome.

r001.rationale: The response describes a possible AI research feedback loop and says 2029 could be consequential, but it does not mention the METR trend or say that a straight-line extrapolation suggests substantial acceleration around 2030.

r002.rationale: The response presents acceleration and bottlenecks as possible outcomes around the same period, but it does not explain that the estimated onset of substantial acceleration overlaps with the estimated onset of substantial deceleration.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish between uncertainty about how fast we get to a particular level of capability and uncertainty about what happens once we get there. Around 2029, you could imagine AI systems becoming good enough at AI research that they substantially accelerate further progress. Better systems help build the next generation, and that creates a feedback loop.

But that isn’t automatic. Perhaps they can write code very well but still struggle to choose useful experiments or carry out a research project reliably. Or perhaps the bottleneck shifts to things like running experiments and getting more compute, which you can’t speed up just by having more automated researchers.

So I wouldn’t interpret 2029 as a precise date when something has to happen. The important question is how much of the process of improving AI can itself be automated, and how much the remaining bottlenecks matter. That’s why I think both a sharp acceleration and a significant slowdown deserve serious consideration.

r001.rationale: The response mentions substantial AI acceleration around 2029, but does not attribute that timing to a straight-line extrapolation of the METR trend.

r002.rationale: It places possible substantial acceleration and significant slowdown in the same around-2029 timeframe, conveying that their timing overlaps.
